• Trap: Students may assume that any jaundice requires immediate intervention.

• Trap: Some may think that switching to breastfeeding can resolve jaundice.

• Trap: There may be an inclination to investigate liver function immediately.
• Why it fails here: Liver function tests are not the first step; bilirubin levels provide more immediate insight into jaundice severity.
• Remember: Liver function tests are reserved for cases where there is suspicion of liver disease or if jaundice persists despite appropriate management.

## NP clinical pathway (Assess → Diagnose → Plan → Evaluate)

1. Assess the infant's age and clinical presentation, noting the persistent jaundice and weight loss.

3. Plan to check the bilirubin level and plot it on a nomogram to determine the need for intervention.
4. Evaluate the results to decide if phototherapy or other interventions are necessary.

## Clinical pearl

Always assess bilirubin levels in infants with jaundice to guide management; plotting on a nomogram is essential for determining treatment needs.

## High-yield facts

• Physiological jaundice is common in newborns, typically resolving by 1-2 weeks of age.
• Bilirubin levels should be monitored closely in infants with jaundice, especially if they are formula-fed.
• Nomograms help assess the risk of hyperbilirubinemia based on age and bilirubin levels.

## Common pitfalls

• Confusing physiological jaundice with pathological jaundice, which requires different management.
• Assuming that all jaundice requires immediate intervention without assessing bilirubin levels first.
• Overlooking the importance of hydration and feeding in managing jaundice.

Monitor for signs of worsening jaundice, such as lethargy or poor feeding, which may indicate the need for urgent intervention.
